tagline: James to York, on river gravel, with the geese in charge.
intro: From Jamestown Island the parkway leaves the James for Williamsburg, slips under the old capital in a tunnel and comes out to run along the York to Yorktown. There are no traffic lights and no lane lines. The pavement is rounded river gravel set in concrete, which gives it an earthy color, and the culverts and underpasses are dressed in brick laid in English and Flemish bond.

Between Williamsburg and Yorktown the road crosses Navy land that was once Penniman, a DuPont shell-loading town of the First World War. The 23 miles took until 1957 to finish. Canada geese on foot have the right-of-way.

moments.title: Historic Jamestowne
moments.text: Jamestown was a peninsula in 1607, and weather later cut it off, so the parkway builders of the 1950s rebuilt the isthmus to get the road onto the island.

moments.title: Colonial Williamsburg
moments.text: The tunnel under the historic district was finished by 1942, then waited out the war and some flooding troubles before the first cars went through in 1949.

moments.title: Yorktown
moments.text: The York River end of the road, where Cornwallis surrendered in 1781, is a town of 221 people that held almost 2,000 around 1750.

practical: Closed to trucks and commercial vehicles other than passenger buses. The limit is 45 mph on most of the parkway and 35 mph in places, and the park posts construction updates on its website.
